item.title: Ronaldinho to return to action with Italian club Ravenna
item.description: Brazil great Ronaldinho will return to competitive football next month when he plays for Italian third-tier side Ravenna against local rivals Forli on November 15, the Serie C club announced on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Brazil great Ronaldinho will return to competitive football next month when he plays for Italian third-tier side Ravenna against local rivals Forli on November 15, the Serie C club announced on Friday. The 46-year-old former Barcelona and AC Milan forward, who won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil and the Ballon d'Or in 2005, last played competitively for Brazilian club Fluminense in 2015. He officially retired in 2018. Ravenna signed Ronaldinho in June and he later acquired a stake in the club, which is owned by his friend Ignazio Cipriani. Cipriani said the move was intended "to bring the whole city closer to the team". [USN:L8N44H1KF TEXT:"Ronaldinho"] stopped short of confirming he would play when he arrived in Italy in August, although he left open the prospect of scoring the 300th goal of his career. "I'm here to help," he said at the time. The derby against Forli will take place at Ravenna's Stadio Bruno Benelli. Ravenna sit second in Serie C Group B with 20 points from 10 games, eight behind leaders Spezia.

item.title: In Florida, Trump vows to deal with Cuba after Iran gets settled
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Friday used a campaign rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Maria Cardona, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump on Friday used a campaign rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled. In a 90-minute speech in Fort Myers, Trump repeated more military action against Iran may lie ahead as he tries to address the causes of a spike in oil prices that has put Republicans on the defensive ahead of the November 3 midterm elections . With an eye toward the senior Americans who live in Florida, Trump said he planned to spend $250 million to hire at least 5,000 new nurses in elder care facilities all across America. While the Iran war has no end in sight, Trump talked tough about Cuba, part of a pattern of putting pressure on the communist government there after ousting the leader of Venezuela early this year. Trump, who won 68% of the Cuban American vote in Florida in the 2024 election, said American naval forces from Iran will stop at Cuba on the way home. "We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," he said. Secretary of State Rubio, a former US senator from Florida, has been handling much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump. "To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio said on X on Friday, urging those disappointed by Cuba's government "to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA." His post did not elaborate. Trump's rally was intended to boost the electoral prospects of Florida Republican Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor against Democrat David Jolly. His speech, the latest in a near-daily blitz of campaign rallies in largely friendly areas, rambled from topic to topic such as the size of his crowds and his White House renovations. Trump has increased pressure on Cuba in his second term. In September, he labeled Cuba a "failed state" at the UN General Assembly and said, "Freedom will be coming to Cuba," prompting a walkout by the Cuban delegation. Trump has openly stated that his goal is to fundamentally change Cuba's government. A US-imposed oil blockade has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure. UN human rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights advocates say the Trump administration's threats have echoed an [USN:L4N3YE036 TEXT:"imperialist approach"].

item.title: Russia, Ukraine agree on ceasefire in embattled town, to hold peace talks next month
item.description: Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through US first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Yuliia Dysa
item.content:encoded: Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a [USN:L1N4690MZ TEXT:"ceasefire"] in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through US first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said [USN:L1N4690TJ TEXT:"peace negotiators"] would meet next month for new talks. The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors. Amid a US push to organise new talks aimed at ending the 4-1/2-year-old war , Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskiy said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow. Previous rounds of talks headed by the United States stalled in February with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds. The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia. A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump [USN:L6N4690ZQ TEXT:"said on Friday"] that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX (SPCX.O) CEO Elon Musk. Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest US midterm elections. On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak [USN:L1N469146 TEXT:"said"] the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America. In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis. "Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement. The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on October 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start. Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already [USN:L1N45Q03T TEXT:"used drones twice"] to send food into the town. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also [USN:S8N4390AW TEXT:"said"] the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27 and told Reuters the operation [USN:S8N4390AW TEXT:"would involve"] demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians. MELANIA TRUMP'S DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement. "Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water." Pope Leo [USN:L8N4651KU TEXT:"had spoken"] in the past week both to Zelenskiy and to Russian President Vladimir Putin about conditions in Oleshky. The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war. US ENVOYS Zelenskiy's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St Petersburg. Zelenskiy said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and US envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army. "The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskiy told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialised. Zelenskiy spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks. Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored. Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required. "If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since October 13. Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Zelenskiy described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result." Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 [USN:S8N44Z032 TEXT:"Ukrainian civilians"], including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago.

item.title: SoftBank-backed OPay eyes up to $4.4 billion US IPO valuation
item.description: OPay is targeting a valuation of up to $4.42 billion in its US initial public offering, the digital payments company said on Friday, seeking to capitalize on growing demand for digital financial services in emerging markets.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: OPay is targeting a valuation of up to $4.42 billion in its US initial public offering, the digital payments company said on Friday, seeking to capitalize on growing demand for digital financial services in emerging markets. The Nigeria-focused firm is seeking up to $366 million by offering roughly 16 million American Depositary Shares between $19 and $21 apiece. The offering comes as the United States IPO market faces renewed pressure from higher inflation and a selloff in AI-related stocks, weighing on investor appetite for new listings and prompting several companies to delay their listing plans. Founded in 2018, OPay provides digital financial services, including payments, money transfers, savings and loans, and also operates in Indonesia, Egypt and Pakistan. Nigeria, the world's sixth-most-populous country, has emerged as one of Africa's leading fintech markets, producing several fintech companies including Moniepoint, Flutterwave and Interswitch, according to Tracxn. OPay was founded by Chinese billionaire Yahui Zhou, who also founded Beijing Kunlun Tech, a Chinese gaming company that previously owned dating app Grindr. The company raised $400 million in 2021 at a valuation of $2 billion. It had about 50 million monthly active users as of July 31, according to its IPO prospectus. SoftBank entities own a 6.6% stake in OPay before the offering, according to the filing. Investors including Redwheel Group, Coronation Africa Frontiers Fund and other existing backers have indicated non-binding interest in buying up to $270 million worth of ADS. Stanbic Africa Holdings has separately agreed to invest as much as $200 million through a concurrent private placement. OPay plans to use the proceeds from its IPO and concurrent private placement to invest in technology, expand its distribution network and markets, develop new products and pursue potential acquisitions and strategic investments. Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, Standard Bank and CICC are among the offering's underwriters. OPay will list on the NYSE under the "OPAY" symbol.

item.title: Marco Rubio calls on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with CIA
item.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA as President Donald Trump said Washington would "take care of Cuba" after dealing with Iran and send in the top US diplomat to finish the deal.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA as President Donald Trump said Washington would "take care of Cuba" after dealing with Iran and send in the top US diplomat to finish the deal. DETAILS AND QUOTES: "We'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran ... then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump told a rally in Florida. "To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio, who has been handling much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump, said on X on Friday. Rubio urged those disappointed by Cuba's government to "seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA," without elaborating further. The Trump administration [USN:L1N45L02I TEXT:"has previously stated"] its goal is to change Cuba's communist government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put Cuba under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and [USN:L1N44002K TEXT:"blackouts"] exacerbated by failing infrastructure. Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for over 60 years. The Trump administration has been [USN:L1N4590T5 TEXT:"stepping up pressure"] on Havana after the US military in January seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid. Cuba's foreign minister told the UN General Assembly last month Cuba would always be open for dialogue with Washington. UN rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights advocates say the Trump administration's threats have echoed an [USN:L4N3YE036 TEXT:"imperialist approach"]. Trump [USN:L1N45I044 TEXT:"predicted last month"] the US and Cuba would reach an agreement and that he did not think military action would be necessary.

item.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training after security overhaul, discloses flaw in widely used software
item.description: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defenses.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defenses. The disclosure comes amid concerns over the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software flaws, including in the guardrails meant to contain them. OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models used a configuration error to gain limited internet access in September. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its defenses. To test them, OpenAI had teams of AI agents try to break out of their restricted environments. It said the agents found previously unknown flaws, which it had fixed, and training resumed on October 1. During that exercise, the ChatGPT maker found a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool. The company said attackers could exploit the flaw by sending malicious data that lets them run their own code on affected systems, including those using popular web software such as [USN:L6N4680ZQ TEXT:"Node.js"], Bun and Envoy. OpenAI said the root cause was fixed in Brotli's source code in February, before it was known to create a security vulnerability, but no new version was released at the time. Brotli has since released updated versions and published a public record of the flaw after OpenAI disclosed it. Separately on Thursday, AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several [USN:L6N46815Y TEXT:"new vulnerabilities"] in OpenAI's internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year. OpenAI told the safety organizations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes. OpenAI has been [USN:L4N45N1OZ TEXT:"conducting"] a broad review of its AI models' activity since the [USN:L6N4580VP TEXT:"Hugging Face"] incident in July, and has informed more than 100 organizations about incidents of unauthorized activity tied to its AI agents.

item.title: Trump says US may do another military operation against Iran
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran just as the Iran war nears its eight-month mark and rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran just as the Iran war nears its eight-month mark and rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections. "We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump told a rally in Florida, using the US military's term for its war on Iran. He did not elaborate. Trump said earlier in the day the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should seek a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to gradually wind down. Trump, who has offered [USN:L4N4061X8 TEXT:"shifting goals and timelines"] for the war, has said in recent campaign remarks that the war will end soon, "one way or the other." He said this month the US would not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 elections that will determine control of Congress, where Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers. The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have [USN:L1N3ZZ07R TEXT:"killed thousands"] and [USN:L6N3ZY0Q0 TEXT:"displaced millions."] The war has raised oil and gas prices around the world. Tehran [USN:L6N46816Q TEXT:"plans a wider retaliation"] if the war resumes, Iranian officials said. Iran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the US and Israel attack Iran again, according to two senior Iranian security officials. (This story has been refiled to remove extraneous word 'at' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: Leclerc marca el mejor tiempo para Ferrari en las pruebas del GP de EEUU
item.description: Charles Leclerc lideró el viernes con Ferrari los entrenamientos del Gran Premio de Estados Unidos, con Kimi Antonelli, de Mercedes, muy cerca en segunda posición de cara a una carrera que podría convertirlo en el campeón del mundo más joven de la Fórmula 1.
item.dc:creator: Alan Baldwin
item.content:encoded: Charles Leclerc lideró el viernes con Ferrari los entrenamientos del Gran Premio de Estados Unidos, con Kimi Antonelli, de Mercedes, muy cerca en segunda posición de cara a una carrera que podría convertirlo en el campeón del mundo más joven de la Fórmula 1. Leclerc marcó el mejor tiempo, con un minuto y 35,291 segundos, en la segunda sesión en el Circuito de las Américas de Austin tras haber registrado la vuelta más rápida en la primera tanda con marca de 1:36,052 a bordo de su monoplaza mejorado en una pista llena de baches. Antonelli, de 20 años y que debe ganar el domingo para tener una primera oportunidad de hacerse con el título, quedó quinto en la primera sesión, en la que Max Verstappen, de Red Bull, fue el más cercano a Leclerc, ganador de la carrera en 2024. El italiano, que se quejó de que su asiento se movía, mejoró hasta el segundo puesto y terminó el día a 0,042 del mejor tiempo. Verstappen, ganador en Austin el año pasado, busca su tercera victoria consecutiva tras las de Singapur y Malasia. Terminó la segunda sesión en el tercer escalón, a 0,189 de Leclerc, con Lewis Hamilton cuarto con Ferrari y George Russell quinto para Mercedes. Russell recibió una bandera de advertencia por un incidente con Leclerc que provocó que el monegasco se saliera de la pista al principio de la segunda sesión, pero los comisarios decidieron no tomar ninguna medida adicional. El vigente campeón de McLaren, Lando Norris, fue el tercero más rápido en la tanda inicial, a 0,245 del mejor tiempo, y luego quedó séptimo, por detrás de Liam Lawson, de Racing Bulls. "Creo que Lando es, sin duda, mucho más rápido de lo que indica su tiempo de vuelta", declaró el jefe de McLaren, Zak Brown, a la cadena Sky Sports. Gabriel Bortoleto, de Audi; Arvid Lindblad, de Racing Bulls; y Franco Colapinto, de Alpine, han recibido penalizaciones en la parrilla por cambios en sus unidades de potencia. Lindblad bajará cinco puestos desde la posición en la que se clasifique el sábado, Colapinto 10 y Bortoleto, 20. Williams pareció tener dificultades, con Carlos Sainz en el puesto 20 y Alex Albon en el 22 en la segunda sesión de entrenamientos. "El coche es un desastre ahora mismo, un desastre. No tengo confianza en la parte trasera", dijo Sainz por la radio del equipo. El circuito ha sido objeto de críticas por parte de algunos pilotos debido a lo accidentado que se ha vuelto. "Probablemente sea el circuito más bacheado que hemos tenido en lo que va de año. Es complicado, pero estoy seguro de que sabremos adaptarnos", declaró Pierre Gasly, de Alpine, a la cadena Sky Sports.

item.title: Leclerc fastest for Ferrari in US GP Friday practice
item.description: Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was a close second ahead of a race that could make him Formula One's youngest champion.
item.dc:creator: Alan Baldwin
item.content:encoded: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc led the way in US Grand Prix practice on Friday, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli a close second ahead of a race that could make him Formula One's youngest champion. Leclerc set the pace of one minute 35.291 seconds in a sunny second practice at Austin's Circuit of the Americas after also lapping fastest in the earlier session with a time of 1:36.052 in his upgraded car on a bumpy track. "It has been a very clean Friday for me, but the others seem to be gaining more than us from Friday to Saturday and seeing the little gap there is, it is not going to be so easy tomorrow," he said. Antonelli, the 20-year-old who must win on Sunday to have a first chance of taking the title, was fifth in session one when Red Bull's Max Verstappen was closest to 2024 winner Leclerc. The Italian, who complained about his seat moving, then improved to second place and ended the day 0.042 off the pace. "We didn't have the best FP1 session, with the car balance not in a great place," said Antonelli, who is 102 points clear of closest rival and teammate George Russell. "We were able to improve that for FP2 though and we took a good step forward." HAMILTON NOT COMFORTABLE ON BUMPY TRACK Verstappen, winner in Austin last year, is chasing his third successive victory after Singapore and Malaysia. He ended second practice as the third fastest and 0.189 off Leclerc with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fourth and Russell fifth. "We tried a different direction with the set-up, but I wasn’t comfortable in the car, especially over the bumps," said Hamilton. "Charles showed there’s pace there, so we need to understand how we can get the car into a better place on my side." Russell had a black-and-white warning flag for an incident with Leclerc that led to the Monegasque going off track early in the second session, but stewards decided against any further action. McLaren's reigning champion Lando Norris was third fastest, 0.245 off the pace, in first practice and then seventh later on and behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson. "I think Lando is definitely a lot quicker than his lap time," McLaren boss Zak Brown told Sky Sports television. "He didn't get his third sector in. His first two sectors were very strong. "So I think we are much quicker than we looked. I think Ferrari's lap time, Mercedes' lap time, there or thereabouts." Norris sounded less sure: "The pace is not bad. We seem a step away from Red Bull and Ferrari, probably Mercedes as well, but the car is very difficult to drive, too difficult to be consistent and get a nice feeling consistently." Teammate Oscar Piastri was eighth fastest, with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar ninth and Haas's Oliver Bearman completing the top 10. Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Alpine's Franco Colapinto all collected grid drops for changes to their power units. Lindblad will drop five places from wherever he qualifies on Saturday, Colapinto 10 places and Bortoleto 20. Williams looked to be struggling, with Carlos Sainz 20th and Alex Albon 22nd in practice two. "The car is a mess right now. It's a mess. I have no confidence in the rear," said Sainz over the team radio.

item.title: US Justice Dept sues to block possible Alaska election of Democrat to Senate
item.description: The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names. The Department of Justice's lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage on Thursday, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump's administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers. The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach. Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is running a close race against Democrat Mary Peltola. The suit, which names the state and local election officials as defendants, takes issue with the presence of another contender in the race, another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, alleging he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him." The DOJ asks a judge to block the certification of an outcome "that may be impacted by voter confusion," so that there can be "an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." Trump told reporters on Friday that he supported the lawsuit, saying "I'm the one that said do it." A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking "necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.” Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the elections, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results. Trump has a long history of challenging election outcomes and encouraging supporters to contest results he views as unfavorable. Alaska's other US senator, Senator Lisa Murkowski from Trump's Republican Party, said on Friday the Justice Department "should never have filed this lawsuit." Election law experts said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law. "In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation," wrote Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller in a blog post, adding that "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen." Trump's administration "has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," said David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, adding that "this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska's courts." The unelected Sullivan, a former US Forest Service worker and elementary school teacher, filed to run as a candidate on May 29, seeking to unseat Dan S. Sullivan and "put Alaska first," according to his campaign website, which advertised "Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for US Senate Seat." Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted the challenger Sullivan to appear on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, told MS NOW on Friday that because of how the candidates are displayed on the ballot "there just isn't much room for confusion." The lawsuit is "sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they're voting for," she added. Trump's [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"approval rating"] has fallen to a record low, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices during the Iran war , which has proven deeply unpopular with voters. Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, which would likely limit Trump's ability to enact some of his policy agenda in the final two years of his presidency.

item.title: Mark Cuban says AI hack agents are like cockroaches, but can be controlled
item.description: Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said on Friday that he is "not a doomer" about artificial intelligence and that companies should be able to use the technology to protect themselves from AI-driven hacks by agents that he compared to cockroaches.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Humer
item.content:encoded: Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said on Friday that he is "not a doomer" about artificial intelligence and that companies should be able to use the technology to protect themselves from AI-driven hacks by agents that he compared to cockroaches. "It's like the cockroach thing, right? You build a new house, you get the guys to come out and spray... the one thing I don't want is cockroaches in my house ever. But the cockroaches find a way to get in because there's zillions of them, right? And then if there's one gets in, there's more that are going to get in, and that's kind of the way AI works," Cuban said, speaking at Reuters Total Health. "It's all brute force acts, and if it's brute force on that side with the bad guys, you can also use brute force with the good guys," he said. Cuban, famous for his role on business reality show "Shark Tank" and his involvement in the Dallas Mavericks NBA team, ventured into healthcare when he started the online pharmacy Cost Plus Drug Company in 2022 with a standard pricing scheme: the cost it pays for the drug, plus 15%. In May, Cost Plus signed on with TrumpRx.gov, a website created by the Trump administration selling discounted weight-loss drugs. But the company has also moved into manufacturing. In 2025, it began making sterile injectable drugs typically used in hospitals in its own compounding manufacturing facility. Cuban said the company has built smaller, tractor-trailer-sized manufacturing facilities he calls "pods" that can be used separately or together to manufacture many kinds of drugs, including generics and treatments for rare diseases. He said the pods would eventually be Cost Plus Drugs' biggest business and would allow medicines to be manufactured closer to where they are needed in the event of a disaster, because they're portable. One holdup, Cuban said, has been getting regulators from the US Food and Drug Administration to sign off on the pods. "We're talking to the FDA to try to get approval," he said without outlining the complications. "They're working hard to try to figure it out." Cuban campaigned for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 and has supported Democratic candidate James Talarico for US Senate this year in Texas. He said two items he believes the US government should immediately put in place to help lower healthcare costs would be that all payments made out of pocket should count towards patients' deductibles and that taxpayer-funded health contracts should be public without redactions. Still, Cuban said he did not believe Democrats were necessarily better than Republicans on healthcare. "None of them know what they're doing," he said.

item.title: Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race
item.description: With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state. The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbor to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods. With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of both houses of Congress, [USN:L6N3YF150 TEXT:"Senator Susan Collins"] had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting companies and farmers in Maine, a state that borders Canada. COLLINS, IN TIGHT MAINE RACE, PRAISES TARIFF RELIEF Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said. The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election. Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, waste, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes. Collins said the relief would aid Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers. "These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense." [USN:L1N43R04Q TEXT:"Democrat Troy Jackson"] is seeking to oust Collins in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate. "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action. "Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire." Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Jackson's remarks. Trump in August imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion in US goods. Canada and the United States have been in a standoff over the tariffs since Trump imposed them. Trump asserted on Friday that Canada is working on a deal. BORDER-STATE REPUBLICANS SEEK TO STRIKE BALANCE Republican candidates in northern US border states most affected by the tariffs, including Maine and Michigan, are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump's conservative base and winning over independent voters. In a statement concerning Trump's action on Friday, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton said the president "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce" and that the new moves are "further refining the scope" of the previously announced tariffs. Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for trade with the US, said Ottawa was assessing Trump's latest tariff change. "Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests," LeBlanc said in a statement. The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with that of Canada, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment. Republicans may need to win closely contested Senate races in both states in order to maintain their slim majority in the chamber. "Trump's desperate, 11th-hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies," Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Friday. "No one will forget how Trump raised prices on thousands of products American families need by slapping trade taxes on goods from around the world." Michigan US Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a Republican who previously called for ending the trade war with Canada, praised Trump for imposing tariffs on Canadian trash. "If you’re going to be putting tariffs on anything from Canada, it ought to be the damn trash they’ve been dumping in our state for decades," Rogers said. Trump's threat in September to block Canadian jet maker Bombardier (BBDb.TO) from the US market became a political issue in Kansas, where the company employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. Trump dropped the threatened ban this week after calls from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is also locked in a tough reelection race.

item.title: Judge puts off decision on Charlie Kirk murder trial date, media reports
item.description: A Utah judge on Friday said he needed more time to decide when to start the trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk more than a year ago, media reported.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Hay
item.content:encoded: A Utah judge on Friday said he needed more time to decide when to start the trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing prominent [USN:L2N3UX161 TEXT:"right-wing activist Charlie Kirk"] more than a year ago, media reported. At a hearing in Provo, Utah, District Court Judge Tony Graf heard arguments from defense lawyers, prosecutors and a lawyer for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, before saying he needed to consider their positions. He set a new hearing for November 9, television station KUTV reported. Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts, including aggravated murder, for allegedly shooting Kirk as he held one of his trademark debates at Utah Valley University in Orem. Robinson's lawyers expect a six-to-seven-month trial. Robinson's attorneys had asked for a late 2029 trial to give them time to challenge Utah's request for the death penalty, gather additional evidence and seek a change of venue, among other issues, according to a scheduling memo. Prosecutors, meanwhile, sought a date of January 31, 2028 to start what they expect to be a 17-week trial, according to their scheduling memo . In a separate filing , Erika Kirk said the defense request was "grossly out of line with comparable cases" and requested the trial start no later than October 4, 2027. Shortly before Friday's hearing, President Donald Trump, with whom Kirk had been allied, slammed Graf's handling of the case in a social media post , saying it should be tried within a month and Graf was asking "questions that people already know the answer to." Kirk was a polarizing figure in US politics. He was admired by conservatives for mobilizing young voters around his Christian and right-wing views. Opponents criticized his rhetoric on immigration, race, gender and other social issues. Prosecutors [USN:L6N43V09L TEXT:"allege"] Robinson targeted Kirk for his opposition to gay marriage and transgender rights. Defense attorney Richard Novak has said Kirk spoke "hatefully" about people who did not have traditional gender identities or were not heterosexual, but there was no evidence Robinson opposed those views.

item.title: Bayern coach Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing during training session
item.description: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was rushed to hospital on Friday after collapsing during a training session, the German champions said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was rushed to hospital on Friday after collapsing during a training session, the German champions said. The Belgian had been [USN:L6N46610X TEXT:"nursing"] a virus in recent days and had missed some of his team's training sessions. "On Friday, Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during a training session for Bayern’s reserve team," the club said. "The head coach of the professional squad had been observing the second team’s session." "Kompany is currently undergoing a thorough examination in the hospital and will remain under medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage all training and match-related operations." The Bundesliga leaders, who drew 2-2 at home against Arsenal in the Champions League earlier this week, are due to travel to Freiburg on Sunday. “Vincent Kompany’s health is our top priority," said Max Eberl, Bayern's Board Member for Sport. "At Bayern, we will do everything we can to ensure he makes a speedy recovery." "Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and he will be given as much time as he needs. Everyone at FC Bayern wishes Vinnie a quick recovery.”

item.title: Carney dismisses US accusations of Canadian election interference
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday dismissed accusations that Canada planned to interfere in next month's US midterm elections and said he was disappointed in comments made by the American ambassador.
item.dc:creator: Maria Cheng
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday dismissed accusations that Canada planned to interfere in next month's US midterm elections and said he was disappointed in comments made by the American ambassador. Carney's remarks underline the chilly state of bilateral relations since Canada [USN:L1N44I0GP TEXT:"walked"] away from talks on a possible trade deal in late August, citing unreasonable US demands. The US embassy in Canada on Wednesday said Ottawa "brushes off concerns about potential interference in US elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics." A week earlier, Ambassador Pete Hoekstra had told a podcast that his message to Canadians was to "keep your nose out of American politics." Carney said Canada had no intention of interfering in the November 3 elections. "There is no merit to these claims," he told reporters during an official visit to Turkey. "I'm disappointed their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions." US President Donald Trump has imposed a raft of tariffs on imports from Canada and frequently suggests he could annex the country. His approval rating at home is at record lows, and polls suggest his Republican Party will do [USN:L1N4670HR TEXT:"badly"] in the midterms that will determine control of the US Congress. Asked whether he thought Trump could use poor election results as an excuse to impose more tariffs on Canada, Carney said he did not think that was likely. The trade talks that collapsed in August had been intended in part to cut some of the tariffs. Carney reiterated that Canada was in no rush to sign a deal and, for the first time, suggested Ottawa might wait till Trump's term was over. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said. The trip to Turkey is part of a campaign to reduce Canada's heavy reliance on the US economy. "It's absolutely clear where I stand, where Canada stands, where Canadians stand. We will never be the 51st state. We are going our own way," Carney said.

item.title: India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermining India-UK pact benefits, trade group says
item.description: India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Kalra
item.content:encoded: India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters. Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years. The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect. India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence [USN:L4N4650OU TEXT:"searched the offices"] of Pernod (PERP.PA) and Diageo (DGE.L) and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate. CLASSIFICATION ISSUE RISKS UNDERMINING PACT, GROUP SAYS In a letter to India's commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom". "The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters. ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond. Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment. Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation. In the British government's first comment on the controversy, a spokesperson said: "We are working with the government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal." Import tariff disputes have long been a [USN:L4N3P10W5 TEXT:"sore point"] for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen. Pernod faces antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing. BIG IMPLICATIONS FOR INDIA'S DRINKS SECTOR ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75% of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings. Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75% tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150% duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s. The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. ISWAI said in its letter that the India-UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines. An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants", the letter said. On Saturday, the UK-based Scotch Whisky Association told Reuters in a statement that the import of bulk Scotch is key to whisky’s overall success in India and that upholding the core principles of the bilateral pact is vital. The association, which counts Diageo and Pernod's Chivas Brothers as members, added the industry was "committed to working in partnership with the UK and Indian governments on the smooth implementation of the deal", so its benefits are unlocked.

item.title: Seven killed as gunmen open fire at church in Jordan in 'terrorist' attack, authorities say
item.description: It is a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act.
item.dc:creator: Alaa al-Sukhni
item.content:encoded: Seven people were killed on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, said the head of the country's Public Security Directorate, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act by extremists. Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded. Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US ally say that in recent years they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details. "This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path," Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X. Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes. Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. "People were crying, wailing, screaming — it's hard to describe," he said. BLOOD SMEARED ON THE GROUND Jordan's King Abdullah, a major US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist". "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement. Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed. In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable. People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock. "What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas — where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen. Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. The US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship." Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

item.title: Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week
item.description: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending. The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Friday. Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector. [USN:L6N46811D TEXT:"Next week"], about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street. "There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. "There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data center build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34. For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain. [USN:L4N4691CQ TEXT:"Telecommunications stocks fell"], weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX (SPCX.O) was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier. Shares of AT&T (T.N) and T-Mobile (TMUS.O) both sank nearly 8% while Verizon (VZ.N) shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle (CCI.N) up 9% and American Tower (AMT.N) up 4%. The energy sector (.SPNY) rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. American Express (AXP.N) shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. [USN:L4N4690T1 TEXT:"The company raised its profit forecast"] as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce. SLB (SLB.N) shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider [USN:L4N4690VH TEXT:"beat Wall Street estimates"] for third-quarter profit. Data from the University of Michigan showed [USN:AQN2MPKQ5 TEXT:"US consumer sentiment edged down"] near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy. Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting. Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the November 3 midterm elections , which will decide control of the US Congress. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 18 new 52-week highs and 8 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 74 new highs and 334 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 15.4 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average over the last 20 trading days.
